objects.name: CTFT Project
objects.description: Capture-The-Flag Techniques - an ontology of CTF solving behaviour. Relates to MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC and CWE as per-entry anchors; not a parallel ATT&CK. Generalized from FOM.

objects.name: IoT / Embedded
objects.description: Hiding/recovering flags inside internet-connected devices: consumer firmware images and their embedded web stacks, IoT messaging brokers (MQTT/CoAP), on-board serial consoles, short-range device radio (Zigbee/BLE/sub-GHz), and the emulation of embedded binaries (MIPS/ARM). Distinct from HWR (electronic badges without a network story), ICS (industrial control systems) and SDR (generic RF signal puzzles): the subject here is the consumer/connected device and its firmware-to-cloud chain. (HTB: Misc (IoT))

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-001 - Vendor firmware image with hardcoded secrets
objects.description: The flag is a hardcoded secret inside a device firmware image: a credential, key or flag string baked into the vendor squashfs, a config blob, or an embedded database. The image is handed over as an opaque blob (or fetched off the device); the concealment is the packaging itself — multiple filesystems, offsets and compression layers — plus the assumption the player will not carve the rootfs.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-001 - Unpack the firmware image and grep the rootfs for secrets
objects.description: 1. Identify the image type and embedded filesystems: binwalk <image>, note offsets and compression (gzip/lzma/xz/squashfs/cramfs). 2. Extract recursively (binwalk -e, then unsquashfs on the carved rootfs) until a real filesystem tree appears. 3. Grep the tree for secrets: credentials, private keys, URLs, flag{-like strings and shadow/passwd entries; check /etc, init scripts and bundled config databases. 4. Validate against the device: recovered credentials should log into the admin interface or unlock the next stage.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-002 - Device web-admin backdoor / default credential gate
objects.description: The device exposes an embedded web stack (lighttpd/uhttpd/Goahead CGI, BusyBox httpd) with a hidden admin route, a magic parameter, or a login that accepts a default credential the UI never mentions. The flag sits behind the backdoor endpoint or a hidden debug page; the concealment is the assumption that players will only interact with the visible interface and never map the embedded server's routes.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-002 - Enumerate the device web stack and abuse its backdoor endpoints
objects.description: 1. Fingerprint the embedded server from banners and error pages (lighttpd, uhttpd, Goahead, BusyBox httpd); each has known debug/maintenance routes. 2. Map routes beyond the UI: content discovery with embedded-device wordlists (cgi-bin/, debug, admin, api, factory, ota), plus parameter fuzzing for magic switches. 3. Try the vendor's documented default credentials on the login; check the firmware image (IOT-001) for the exact credential if login resists. 4. Validate: the backdoor route or debug page yields the flag or the next stage.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-003 - Unauthenticated message-broker topic/queue concealment
objects.description: The ecosystem ships a publish/subscribe or message-queue service that accepts anonymous or weakly-authenticated connections — any broker or bus technology (MQTT, CoAP resources, AMQP, Redis pub/sub, a custom device bus). Data the player needs is stored or transits on non-obvious channels: an unpublished topic, a retained message, a device-shadow update, a dead-letter or administrative queue. The concealment is categorial: everyone treats the broker as dumb infrastructure and nobody thinks to enumerate its namespace as an information repository, the way one would enumerate a filesystem or an API.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-003 - Enumerate broker topics/queues and capture service traffic
objects.description: 1. Identify the service and its protocol from the port and banner (nmap service scan; brokers also answer protocol-native PING/INFO probes). 2. Enumerate the namespace the way the protocol allows: wildcard or catch-all subscriptions where supported (MQTT #), resource discovery endpoints (CoAP .well-known/core), queue/channel listing in management interfaces, or brute-force of channel names from challenge vocabulary. 3. Mine the surrounding artifacts for credentials when auth is required: the firmware image (IOT-001), the device story, vendor defaults — read ACLs are often anonymous even where write is gated. 4. Capture long enough for periodic traffic; retained or scheduled messages usually reveal the channel map without any guesswork. 5. Validate: the data found on the channel satisfies the challenge's flag format.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-004 - On-board serial console flag (UART/JTAG exposure)
objects.description: The flag is only reachable through the device's debug interface: a UART console printing it at boot, a U-Boot shell over serial, or a JTAG-exposed memory region. The concealment is physical — unlabelled pads, an uncommon baud rate, a bootlog that scrolls past — and the assumption that players will not pick up a serial adapter.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-004 - Identify debug pads and read the serial console
objects.description: 1. Locate the debug interface: continuity-scan for TX/RX/GND pads (TX idles high); typical baud rates are 115200, 57600, 38400, 9600. 2. Attach a USB-UART adapter, capture the full boot log — flags are often printed by boot scripts before the console is silenced. 3. If the console offers a U-Boot/bootloader shell, dump the environment (printenv), memory (md) and flash; interrupt the boot to reach it. 4. For JTAG exposure, enumerate the chain and read memory via openocd before attempting anything invasive. 5. Validate: the boot log, env or dump contains the flag or points to the next stage.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-005 - Short-range IoT radio concealment (Zigbee/BLE/sub-GHz)
objects.description: The flag transits a short-range device radio: a Zigbee sensor network, a BLE GATT characteristic or advertisement, or a sub-GHz (433/868 MHz) remote. The concealment is the air interface: the protocol looks opaque, traffic is periodic and low-volume, and the key material (Zigbee network key, BLE pairing) may be recoverable only from the device firmware. Distinct from SDR-001 (generic RF puzzles) and NET-004 (Wi-Fi): the subject is the IoT protocol ecosystem and its device pairing.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-005 - Sniff and decode the device radio protocol
objects.description: 1. Identify the band and protocol from the challenge story and hardware (Zigbee 2.4 GHz OQPSK, BLE advertisements, 433/868 MHz ASK/OOK remotes). 2. Capture: killerbee/ubertooth for Zigbee/BLE, bettercap for BLE GATT, an SDR or rtl433 for sub-GHz remotes. 3. Recover the link keys: Zigbee network keys often ship in the firmware (IOT-001) or via well-known Trust Center defaults; BLE pairing traffic is sniffeable only if captured during pairing — force a re-pair when possible. 4. Decode the frames to application payloads; sensor values and remotes often encode the flag in plain structured bytes. 5. Validate: the decoded payload satisfies the flag format.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.

objects.name: CTFTTE-IOT-006 - Embedded-binary exploitation behind device emulation (MIPS/ARM)
objects.description: The vulnerable service is an embedded binary — a MIPS or ARM build of a device daemon (lighttpd CGI, a custom TCP service) — shipped either as a loose binary or inside the firmware image. The player must first make it run (qemu-user with the right endianness, libs and page size), then exploit a classic memory-corruption bug on an unfamiliar architecture. The concealment is the emulation barrier plus the architecture: gadgets, calling conventions and exploit primitives all differ from x86.

objects.name: CTFTCTE-IOT-006 - Emulate the service and exploit the embedded binary
objects.description: 1. Identify the architecture and endianness (file, ELF header) and the interpreter/libc dependencies (MIPS/ARM musl or uClibc builds differ from glibc). 2. Emulate with qemu-user: qemu-mips{,el} -L <rootfs> ./service — pull the rootfs from the firmware image (IOT-001) when libs are missing. 3. Reverse the service in Ghidra (MIPS/ARM calling conventions: argument registers $a0-$a3 / r0-r3, delay slots on MIPS); locate the bug exactly as on x86. 4. Build the exploit with pwntools on the target architecture: ROP via gadgets in the binary or libc; mind that syscall conventions and bad bytes differ. 5. Validate: the payload executes on the emulated service and yields the flag or a shell.
Counter-technique recovers/defeats the paired design technique. `mitigates` is kept for STIX-consumer compatibility; the CTFT semantics are carried by x_ctft_relation.
